name: The Balance of Power
statement: States act to keep any one power from dominating, so coalitions form against whoever grows too strong.
meaning: The balance of power is the theory and condition that security is enhanced when military and economic power is distributed among states so that no single state or coalition becomes strong enough to dominate all others. When one power threatens to grow preponderant, other states respond, through arms build-ups, alliances, or ultimately war, to check it, a process that tends to produce a recurring, roughly self-regulating equilibrium in which hegemony is prevented. It is used in two senses: as a description of how states recurrently behave, and as a deliberate policy states pursue to preserve their independence.
mechanism: States check a rising power in two ways. Internal balancing means building up one's own capabilities, through military spending, weapons, and economic strength. External balancing means adding others' power to one's own by forming alliances against the threat. Realist theory expects balancing, aligning against the strongest or most threatening power, to predominate over bandwagoning, joining the stronger side. A flexible offshore state can act as a balancer, throwing its weight to whichever side is weaker; Britain historically played this role in Europe. Structural realists argue balancing recurs because the anarchic system, not the character of states, pushes them to check concentrations of power.

examples.text: Successive anti-French coalitions checked Napoleonic France and, after its defeat, the Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe to prevent renewed French domination, the paradigmatic balancing arrangement.
The US-led and Soviet-led blocs formed a two-pole balance, a case Waltz used to argue that bipolarity could be relatively stable.
Naval supremacy and immunity from invasion let Britain shift its weight to the weaker side in Europe, keeping the system both flexible and stable from the Napoleonic era to the First World War.

variants.name: Balance of threat
variants.text: Stephen Walt's modification that states balance against threat, a compound of power, proximity, offensive capability, and perceived intentions, not against raw power alone, so scary weak states get balanced and benign strong ones may not.

variants.name: Hegemonic stability theory
variants.text: The rival view that a single dominant power can produce stability by providing order and open trade, inverting the intuition that concentrated power is dangerous.

whyItMatters: The balance of power is a foundational realist concept for explaining alliance formation and the recurrence of anti-hegemonic coalitions, why states so often gang up against whoever looks likeliest to dominate. It gives realism a systemic account of stability, war, and alignment that does not depend on the internal makeup of states, and it frames enduring policy debates about hegemony, polarity, and how much order a dominant power can safely be allowed to hold.

working.text: anticipate that a rising power will provoke others to combine against it, whether by arming or by alliance.
distinguish aligning against the strongest, the realist norm, from joining it, treated as the exception.
weigh proximity, offensive capability, and intentions alongside raw strength, since states balance against threat.

limits: The concept is disputed. Balancing sometimes fails: states bandwagon, buck-pass in the hope someone else balances, or appease instead, a pattern Randall Schweller theorised as underbalancing and traced to domestic politics, noting that no great power urgently balanced Nazi Germany in the 1930s. The post-Cold-War unipolar moment did not obviously produce hard balancing against the United States, spawning debates over soft balancing and whether balance-of-power theory holds. It is also criticised as vague, hard to falsify, and inconsistently predictive, and hegemonic stability theory offers the opposite reading of when the system is most peaceful.
misreadings: It does not mean everyone has equal power; it means power is distributed so no one can dominate, and it need not be symmetrical. It is not an automatic law of nature but a tendency, since underbalancing, buck-passing, and appeasement are real and recurrent. It is not always a deliberate policy; neorealists stress it can emerge as an unintended systemic outcome even when no one intends it. And it is not the same as balance of threat, Walt's modification in which states balance against threat rather than raw power. Britain as balancer did not stay neutral; the balancer intervenes on the weaker side.
origin: An ancient idea, from Thucydides and the Renaissance Italian city-states to Hume's 1752 essay 'Of the Balance of Power' and Metternich's Concert of Europe, formalised as a central concept of realism, above all in Kenneth Waltz's structural 'Theory of International Politics' (1979).
